body.en: Exploratory data analysis uses graphical and numerical summaries to describe the distribution of one variable and the relationship between two variables. Always describe shape, center, spread, and outliers (S-C-S-O) in context.

blocks.heading: Level 1 · Foundations — Graphical Displays, Shape, Center & Spread

body.en: Distinguish between categorical and quantitative data, construct and interpret dotplots, stemplots, and histograms, and describe distribution shape.

When describing a quantitative distribution, you must explicitly state all four characteristics in context:

  • Center: Median or mean with units.
  • Unusual features: Mention any apparent outliers or distinct gaps.
  • Spread: Interquartile range (IQR), standard deviation, or range with units.
  • Shape: Skewed right (tail to the right), skewed left (tail to the left), or approximately symmetric (single mound, bimodal, uniform).

A sample of test scores has a mean of 74 and a median of 82. Describe the probable shape of the distribution, explaining the relationship between the mean and median.

Because the mean (74) is substantially less than the median (82), the mean has been pulled downward by extreme low scores in the left tail. Therefore, the distribution is skewed to the left.

question.en:
Level 1 · Foundations

The weights (in ounces) of 8 newborn puppies are: 11, 12, 13, 13, 14, 15, 17, 21. Calculate the median and interquartile range (IQR) of this dataset.

solution.en:
With \(n = 8\) ordered values:

Lower half: \(11, 12, 13, 13\) \(\implies Q_1 = \frac{12 + 13}{2} = 12.5\text{ oz}\).

Upper half: \(14, 15, 17, 21\) \(\implies Q_3 = \frac{15 + 17}{2} = 16.0\text{ oz}\).

Median: middle of 13 and 14: \[ M = \frac{13 + 14}{2} = \mathbf{13.5\text{ oz}}. \]

Interquartile range: \[ \text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1 = 16.0 - 12.5 = \mathbf{3.5\text{ oz}}. \]

blocks.heading: Level 2 · Medium — Outlier Identification, Boxplots & Normal Model z-Scores

body.en: Apply the 1.5 IQR rule for outliers, compare parallel boxplots, and calculate standardized z-scores under the normal distribution.

A point \(x\) is an outlier if:

\[ x < Q_1 - 1.5\cdot\text{IQR} \quad \text{or} \quad x > Q_3 + 1.5\cdot\text{IQR}. \]

The mean and standard deviation are non-resistant (strongly affected by outliers); the median and IQR are resistant. Use median and IQR for skewed distributions or datasets with outliers.

title.en: ⊙ Explorer · Mean vs median — the effect of an outlier

ariaLabel.en: A dot plot of ages 12, 15, 18, 21, 24, and a sixth adjustable outlier value, with markers for the mean and median

caption.en: The six data points, sorted, and the summary statistics

note.en: Five base values: 12, 15, 18, 21, 24. Slide the 6th value: the median barely moves (it stays around 19.5), while the mean tracks the outlier directly. That is the definition of resistant vs non-resistant.

body.en:
A distribution of salaries has \(Q_1 = \$42,000\) and \(Q_3 = \$68,000\). A director earns \(\$110,000\). Is this salary an outlier according to the 1.5 IQR rule?

Compute IQR: \[ \text{IQR} = 68000 - 42000 = 26000. \]

Upper outlier boundary: \[ Q_3 + 1.5(\text{IQR}) = 68000 + 1.5(26000) = 68000 + 39000 = \$107,000. \]

Because \(\$110,000 > \$107,000\), this salary is an outlier.

question.en:
Level 2 · Medium

The heights of adult males in a region follow a normal distribution with mean \(\mu = 70\) inches and standard deviation \(\sigma = 3\) inches. What is the standardized z-score of a male who is 76 inches tall, and what proportion of adult males are taller than 76 inches?

solution.en:
Compute the z-score: \[ z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma} = \frac{76 - 70}{3} = \frac{6}{3} = \mathbf{2.00}. \]

By the Empirical Rule (68-95-99.7%), approximately 95% of data lies within 2 standard deviations of the mean, leaving 5% split between both tails. The upper tail is: \[ P(Z > 2.00) = \frac{1 - 0.95}{2} = 0.025 = \mathbf{2.5\%} \quad (\text{or } 0.0228 \text{ using exact tables}). \]

blocks.heading: Level 3 · Advanced — Bivariate Regression, Residual Analysis & r² Interpretation

body.en: Construct least-squares regression lines, interpret slope and intercept in context, evaluate model adequacy via residual plots, and interpret the coefficient of determination.

Regression equation: \[ \hat{y} = a + bx \quad \text{where slope } b = r\frac{s_y}{s_x} \quad \text{and intercept } a = \bar{y} - b\bar{x}. \]

Residual: \(e_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i\) (Actual \(y\) minus Predicted \(\hat{y}\)).

Residual Plot: A random scatter around \(y = 0\) with no curved pattern indicates a linear model is appropriate.

Coefficient of determination \(r^2\): The percentage of variation in the response variable \(y\) explained by the linear relationship with explanatory variable \(x\).

A regression equation predicting used car price (\(y\), in thousands of dollars) from age (\(x\), in years) is \(\hat{y} = 28.5 - 2.1x\). Interpret the slope \(-2.1\) in context.

Interpretation: For each additional year in the car's age, the predicted price decreases by $2,100 (or 2.1 thousand dollars) on average.

question.en:
Level 3 · Advanced

A linear regression model relating study hours \(x\) to exam score \(y\) yields the equation \(\hat{y} = 45 + 5.2x\). A student who studied 6 hours scored 80 on the exam. (a) Calculate the residual for this student. (b) If \(r^2 = 0.64\), interpret this value in context.

solution.en:
(a) Residual: Compute predicted score: \[ \hat{y} = 45 + 5.2(6) = 45 + 31.2 = 76.2. \] Residual: \[ y - \hat{y} = 80 - 76.2 = \mathbf{+3.8\text{ points}}. \] The student scored 3.8 points higher than predicted by the model.

(b) \(r^2\) Interpretation: Exactly 64% of the variation in exam scores is explained by the linear relationship with the number of study hours.
